questions.prompt: Which statement about an empty `std::optional<int> o;` is correct?
questions.explanation: `operator*` has the precondition that the optional contains a value, so calling it on an empty optional is undefined behavior. `value()` is the checked accessor and throws `bad_optional_access`. Neither returns a default value; `value_or` is the accessor for that.

questions.explanation: A default-constructed variant holds a value-initialized first alternative, here an empty `std::string`, so the index is 0 and the size is 0. It is never empty and never holds an indeterminate `int` instead. If the first alternative were not default constructible, the variant would not be either.

questions.explanation: An empty optional compares less than any value of `T`, so `n < -1` is true. `n == 0` is false because there is no value to equal 0, and `n > 0` is false because an empty optional is never greater than a value. The comparison operators do not dereference, so there is no undefined behavior.

questions.explanation: The converting constructor ignores alternatives that would need a narrowing conversion, and a pointer-to-bool conversion counts as narrowing. That leaves only `std::string`, so the index is 1. Before those changes `bool` won, because a standard conversion beats a user-defined one, which is the tempting answer.

options: Ill-formed: `any` cannot hold a string literal

questions.explanation: An `any` stores the decayed type of its initializer, so `a` holds a `const char*`, not a `std::string`. `any_cast` requires an exact type match and performs no conversion, so it throws `bad_any_cast`. The cast `any_cast<const char*>(a)` would succeed.

questions.explanation: The converting constructor selects an alternative by overload resolution over `F(int)` twice, which is ambiguous, so the constructor does not participate and the initialization is ill-formed. There is no tie-break by position. To pick an alternative explicitly use `std::in_place_index<0>`.

questions.prompt: Is this program well-formed in C++23?
options: Yes; the `any` is simply not copyable
Yes; it holds a copy of the pointee
No: the decayed type must be copy constructible
questions.explanation: The converting constructor of `any` only participates when the decayed type is copy constructible, because the `any` itself must be copyable for whatever it holds. `unique_ptr<int>` is not, so no constructor is viable and the program is ill-formed. A move-only payload is rejected even if you never copy the `any`.
